title: Bees on the roof
context: You will hear a woman called Nadia talking about her work keeping bees on the roofs of office buildings.

unit.style: a relaxed, engaging talk to an audience, at a natural pace

turns.text: Hi everyone. I'm Nadia, and for the past two years I've been looking after beehives on the roofs of office buildings in central London. When people hear that, they usually picture me in a garden, but my first hives were actually on top of an insurance company, eleven floors up, next to the air-conditioning units.

I didn't plan any of this. I studied geography, and I was working in a café when a regular customer, who turned out to be a beekeeper, asked if I'd help him lift some boxes. That was the beginning. He taught me everything, and the first thing he made me learn wasn't about bees at all. It was how to read a weather forecast properly, because you never open a hive when it's cold or about to rain.

People often ask whether the bees mind living so high up. In fact, they seem to do very well. London has more variety of flowers than most farmland, thanks to parks, gardens and even the plants people grow on their balconies. Our honey changes colour through the year. In spring it's pale, almost like lemon juice, and by late summer it's dark, a bit like strong tea, because of the lime trees.

The companies don't keep hives for the honey, of course. Most of them see it as a way to show their staff that they care about the environment. The part I enjoy most is running workshops for employees. I've had senior managers who were terrified at the start, and by the end they're holding a frame covered in bees and asking if they can come back next week.

Looking after the hives takes less time than people imagine. In summer I check each one about once a week, mainly to make sure the colony has enough space and isn't getting ready to leave. In winter there's very little to do, apart from making sure the bees have enough food stored and that nothing has disturbed the boxes. The busiest season is actually spring, when everything seems to happen at once.

It isn't all positive, though. Some scientists worry that there are now too many hives in the city, and that honeybees are competing with wild bees for food. I take that seriously. These days I advise companies to plant flowers before they get a hive, and in a couple of cases I've told a business not to get one at all. That doesn't make me very popular with my employer, but I think it's the right thing to do.

If you're tempted to try beekeeping yourself, my advice is simple: join a local association first, and spend a season helping someone else before you buy anything. And invest in a good pair of gloves. I learnt that the hard way.
